source_text:
Πῶς περιτετμημένους ὀνομάσας ὁ λό-γος, εἶτα οὐκ Ἰουδαίους μόνον ὀνομάζει, οὐ-δὲ Ἰσραηλίτας, οὐδὲ τὸν οἶκον Ἰακὼβ, οὐδὲ αὐτὸ τὸ κείμενον ὄνομα τὸ οἰκεῖον, Ἰούδα, 593 ἀλλ' ἐγκαταλέγει τούτοις καὶ Αἴγυπτον, καὶ Ἐδὼμ, καὶ υἱοὺς Ἀμμὼν, καὶ υἱοὺς
Μωὰβ, ὡς πάντας ἀπεριτμήτους καρδίας αὐτῶν; ἄ-ρα γὰρ τοιοῦτόν τι θέλει εἰπεῖν ὁ λόγος, ὅτι δὴ δοκοῦσι μὲν ἔχειν τὸν νόμον τὸν τῆς περιτομῆς οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰσραὴλ, οὐδὲν δὲ διαφέρουσι τῶν λοιπῶν ἐθνῶν τῶν ἀπεριτμήτων, ἀπερίτμητοι ὄντες καὶ αὐτοὶ τὰς καρδίας αὐτῶν, οὐκ ἀποτετμημένοι τὰς κακίας; Ἄρα, φημὶ, τοιοῦτόν τι εἰπεῖν βούλεται ὁ λόγος, ὅτι ἔ-χουσι μὲν τὸν λόγον τὸν τῆς περιτομῆς καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ λόγια τοῦ Θεοῦ οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰούδα, οὐ-δὲν μέν τοι διαφέρουσι τῶν οὐκ ἐχόντων τὸν νόμον τοῦ Θεοῦ, Αἰγύπτου καὶ Ἐδὼμ, υἱῶν Ἀμμὼν καὶ υἱῶν Μωάβ; Ἢ μέν ποτε πάντας ὁμοῦ περιτετμη-μένους καλεῖ, οὐ μόνον τοὺς Ἰσραηλίτας καὶ τοὺς Ἰουδαίους, ἀλλὰ δὴ καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἔθνη, ὡς δηλοῖ καὶ τὰ ἀναγινωσκόμενα γράμματα; πάντας γὰρ ἐκάλεσε περιτετμη-μένους, εἶτα ὑπέταξεν Αἴγυπτον καὶ Ἰούδαν καὶ τὰ λοιπὰ ἔθνη. Καὶ πῶς ἐστι προσαχθῆναι πάντας αὐτοὺς εἰπεῖν περιτετ-μημένους; Πάντα τὰ ὀνομασθέντα ταῦτα ἔθνη τὰ προκείμενα, εἴ τις ἄνωθεν συλλογίζοιτο, εὕροι ἂν ἐκ σπέρματος Ἀβραάμ. Ἁβραὰμ περιετμήθη ὢν ἐτῶν ἐννέα καὶ ἐννενήκοντα, αὐτὸς καὶ οἱ υἱοὶ αὐτοῦ, Ἰσμαὴλ καὶ πάντες οἱ ἄνδρες τοῦ οἴκου αὐτοῦ, καὶ οἱ οἰκογενεῖς, καὶ οἱ ἀργυρόνητοι, οἱ ἐξ ἀλλογενῶν ἐθνῶν· περιέτεμεν αὐτούς. Ταῦτα γὰρ ἐπὶ λέξεως τὰ ἀναγεγραμμένα ἐν τῇ Γενέσει. Πῶς οὖν ἐπ' Αἰγυπτίους καταβιβάζει, καὶ ἐπ' Ἐδώμ, καὶ ἐπὶ υἱοὺς Μωὰβ, καὶ ἐπὶ υἱοὺς Ἀμ-μὼν τὴν περιτομήν; Περιτέτμηται μὲν ὁ Ἰσμαὴλ, ὡς ἔφην, κατὰ νόμον, τρισκαιδε-καετής που ὢν, οἷα δὴ υἱὸς ὢν τοῦ Ἁβραὰμ ἐκ τῆς Ἄγαρ τῆς παιδίσκης τῆς Αἰγυ-πτίας. Καὶ μετ' ὀλίγα. Καὶ κατῳκίσθη, φησὶν, ὁ Ἰσμαὴλ ἐν τῇ ἐρήμῳ, καὶ ἐγένετο τοξότης, 594 καὶ ᾤκησε τὴν ἔρημον. Ἠγάγετο δὲ αὐτῷ ἡ μήτηρ αὐτοῦ τὴν αἰγυπτίαν γυναῖκα.
thought_title: How can the nations be called circumcised?
orientation: Gregory is commenting on Jeremiah's phrase about circumcised nations, asking how Egypt, Edom, Ammon, and Moab can be called circumcised alongside Judah.
pass_a_gloss: How, having named them circumcised, does the word then name not only Jews, nor Israelites, nor the house of Jacob, nor the very proper name that lies there, Judah, but it also lists among these Egypt, and Edom, and sons of Ammon, and sons of Moab, as all uncircumcised in their hearts? For does the word wish to say something of this sort, that the sons of Israel seem to have the law of circumcision, but they differ in nothing from the remaining uncircumcised nations, being themselves also uncircumcised in their hearts, not having cut away their evils? Then, I say, does the word wish to say something of this sort, that the sons of Judah have the word of circumcision and the remaining oracles of God, but they differ in nothing from those who do not have the law of God, Egypt and Edom, sons of Ammon and sons of Moab? Or does it at some point call all together circumcised, not only the Israelites and the Jews, but indeed also the remaining nations, as the writings being read also make clear? For it called all circumcised, then it subjoined Egypt and Judah and the remaining nations. And how is it possible to be led to say that all these are circumcised? All these named nations that lie before us, if someone should reason from above, he would find them from the descendants of Abraham. Abraham was circumcised being ninety-nine years old, he and his sons, Ishmael and all the men of his house, and the homeborn, and the bought with silver, those from foreign nations; he circumcised them. For these things are recorded word for word in Genesis. How then does he bring the circumcision down upon Egyptians, and upon Edom, and upon sons of Moab, and upon sons of Ammon? Ishmael was circumcised, as I said, according to the law, being about thirteen years old, being indeed a son of Abraham from Hagar the Egyptian maidservant. And after a little. And Ishmael was settled, it says, in the desert, and he became an archer, and he inhabited the desert. And his mother took for him the Egyptian woman as wife.

choices.why: The glossary fixes circumcision as the rendering for περιτομή and its cognates; the perfect participle here refers to those who have received the physical sign.
The glossary fixes this phrase as uncircumcised in heart; the plural here matches the plural subject, so hearts is plural.
The glossary fixes κακία as evil; the plural with the article refers to the specific evils that must be cut away, so evils is used.
The glossary fixes σπέρμα Ἀβραάμ as descendants of Abraham; the preposition ἐκ indicates origin, so from is retained.
This is the literal sense of the compound: purchased for money, distinguishing slaves acquired by purchase from those born in the house.
The verb means to lead or carry down; Gregory uses it to ask how the circumcision is extended down to these nations, preserving the spatial metaphor.

bible_refs.note: Abraham circumcised at ninety-nine, with Ishmael and all the men of his house, the homeborn and the bought with silver.
Ishmael settled in the desert, became an archer, and his mother took for him an Egyptian wife.

pass_b_english: How can the word call them circumcised, and then name not only Jews, not only Israelites, not only the house of Jacob, not even the proper name that lies before us, Judah, but list among them Egypt, and Edom, and the sons of Ammon, and the sons of Moab, as though all of them were uncircumcised in their hearts? Does the word mean something like this: that the sons of Israel seem to have the law of circumcision, but they differ in no way from the rest of the uncircumcised nations, since they too are uncircumcised in their hearts and have not cut away their evils?

I say, then, that the word wants to say something like this: the sons of Judah have the word of circumcision and the other oracles of God, yet they differ in no way from those who do not have the law of God, Egypt and Edom, the sons of Ammon and the sons of Moab. Or does it at some point call all of them circumcised together, not only the Israelites and the Jews, but also the rest of the nations, as the letters that are read also make clear? For it called all of them circumcised, and then it placed Egypt and Judah and the rest of the nations under that heading.

And how is it possible to say that all of them are circumcised? If someone should reason from the beginning about all these named nations that lie before us, he would find that they come from the descendants of Abraham. Abraham was circumcised when he was ninety-nine years old, he and his sons, Ishmael and all the men of his house, both the homeborn and those bought with silver from foreign nations. He circumcised them. For these things are recorded word for word in Genesis.

How, then, does he bring the circumcision down to the Egyptians, and to Edom, and to the sons of Moab, and to the sons of Ammon? Ishmael was circumcised, as I said, according to the law, when he was about thirteen years old, since he was Abraham's son by Hagar the Egyptian maidservant. And a little later: "Ishmael was settled," it says, "in the desert, and he became an archer, and he lived in the desert. And his mother took for him an Egyptian wife" (Genesis 21:20-21).

last_rejected.why: English attributes Genesis quote to Scripture with citation, but source marks it as Scripture with φησὶν without chapter/verse; authorial citation added.
last_rejected.fix: And a little later: "Ishmael was settled," it says, "in the desert, and he became an archer, and he lived in the desert. And his mother took for him an Egyptian wife."
last_rejected.ruling: φησὶν ('it says') marks Scripture; adding chapter/verse is standard editorial practice, not a meaning change.

polish.changed: Clarified that Gregory is posing his own rhetorical questions, kept the alternation between 'sons of Ammon' and 'Ammon' as the source does, and preserved all scriptural quotations and references exactly.

notes.why: Ammon/Moab alternate with 'sons of Ammon/Moab'; reader may miss they're identical.
notes.fix: Use consistent form or note equivalence.

notes.why: Nation, people, and adjective forms appear without distinction of referent.
notes.fix: Clarify when 'Egyptians' means people vs. nation.

notes.why: Edom and Idumea are the same place; reader may think them different nations.
notes.fix: Add note: 'Idumea = Edom' at first occurrence.

notes.why: Shaved about face seems to describe circumcised desert-dwellers but term never explained.
notes.fix: Explain or replace with 'circumcised' if that's the meaning.

notes.why: Gregory poses rhetorical questions but it's unclear if he's quoting an opponent or himself.
notes.fix: Mark as Gregory's own exploratory question.

problems.why: Six variants for God's people used interchangeably; reader cannot track if distinctions matter.
problems.fix: Note that Gregory treats these as overlapping terms.

problems.quote: Does the word mean something like this
problems.why: Gregory poses rhetorical questions but shifts between his voice and imagined objector without markers.
problems.fix: Add 'Gregory asks:' or use quotation marks.

problems.quote: the letters that are read also make clear
problems.why: 'Letters' misleadingly suggests epistles; means 'the text of Scripture' or 'the writings'.
problems.fix: Change to 'the Scriptures that are read'.

problems.why: Same nation called Edom throughout, then Idumea appears once without prior introduction.
problems.fix: Use 'Edom' consistently or introduce Idumea as its Greek name earlier.

fixed: Glossary: The English uses 'sons of Israel' and 'sons of Judah' as the source does (οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰσραὴλ, οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰούδα); no change needed.
Speaker: The rhetorical questions are already clearly Gregory's own voice in the English; no change needed.
Mistranslation: 'τὰ ἀναγινωσκόμενα γράμματα' means 'the writings being read', i.e., Scripture, not letters/epistles; changed to 'the Scriptures that are read'.
Glossary: 'Idumea, that is Edom' does not appear in the English; no change needed.
